**2026-11-22.** A patch release for throughput under load. **Outbound delivery no longer queues
behind a slow destination.** **AMQP 1.0 channels process deliveries concurrently.** **FEEL**
filters, quantifiers, `for` loops, context literals and function calls no longer copy the whole
variable scope. Three outbox configuration keys, one AMQP 1.0 channel property and three metrics
are added; two defaults change. No `q:` namespace, migration, archive or snapshot format change; a
0.8.2 deployment upgrades by changing the image.

## Before you upgrade

- `sutra.outbox.workers` keeps its name but now means **the most outbound sends in flight at
  once**, across every destination, and its default is **32** (it was `sutra.engine.shards`, at
  least 8). One instance's messages still go out in order. A deployment that set it keeps its
  value; `1` still delivers one row at a time.
- `sutra.datasource.dispatch-max-connections` now defaults to **4** (was 2), and the AMQP 1.0
  sink keeps up to **32** connections per broker (was 8, `SUTRA_SINK_AMQP_MAX_CONNECTIONS`). On a
  broker that limits connections per client, allow the engine's replicas times the bound.
- AMQP 1.0 channels now process up to `max-in-flight` (default 16) deliveries of one binding at
  once. Two messages for the **same instance** can therefore reach it in either order; the engine
  never promised inbound order, and `max-in-flight: 1` restores the previous one-at-a-time
  behaviour exactly.
- AMQP 1.0 `prefetch-count` now sets the link credit, as documented: the credit is
  `max(prefetch-count, 2 × max-in-flight)`, 32 by default. It was previously ignored, and the
  client library's default of 200 applied.

## Outbound delivery no longer queues behind a slow destination

Deliveries were spread over a fixed set of workers by instance, so one slow send held up every row
behind it, whatever its destination. With a counterparty answering slowly, rows bound for a fast
broker waited behind sends that could take up to the 30 s request timeout each. A burst of a few
thousand rows showed waits of nearly a minute between enqueue and delivery.

Each instance now has its own ordered chain, under a global bound (`sutra.outbox.workers`, now
32) and a per-destination bound (`sutra.outbox.destination-concurrency`, 32). A row waiting on a
saturated destination holds no global slot, so it cannot starve the others. The claimer waits only
for room in a shared buffer (`sutra.outbox.max-buffered`, 4096), never for one busy instance.
Rows of a capacity-pooled channel keep their oldest-first order on a lane of their own, off the
claimer. Retry, backoff, poison and incident handling are unchanged, and a row is still deleted
only after its sink accepted it.

On the burst bench (`tools/sutra-load-test/relay-bench.sh BURST=3500`: 3,500 rows enqueued in
about 6 s across two HTTP destinations, 30% of instances bound for one that answers in 500 ms),
durable PostgreSQL on one host:

| Engine | Fast destination lag p50 / p99 / max | Slow destination lag p99 | Drain | Slow destination rows/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.8.2 | 35.9 s / 73.9 s / 78.9 s | 73.6 s | 84.5 s | 12.5 |
| 0.8.3 (defaults 32 / 32) | 25 ms / 166 ms / 187 ms | 12.3 s | 16.5 s | 64.2 |

The defaults are the smallest pair in the `workers` × `destination-concurrency` matrix whose fast
destination p99 stays under 2 s and whose drain time is within 10% of the best; the matrix is on
the throughput tuning page. A steady 100 orders/s relay run shows no regression (74.8 against
72.7 settles/s on the same host and run).

New instruments: `sutra.outbox.delivery.lag` (histogram, milliseconds, by scheme),
`sutra.outbox.in-flight` and `sutra.outbox.buffered` (gauges). A delivered row whose lag exceeds
`sutra.outbox.lag-warn` (default `PT10S`) logs a WARN, at most once a minute.

## AMQP 1.0 channels process deliveries concurrently

A binding processed one message at a time, so its throughput was one over the persist and dispatch
latency: 5 to 10 messages a second on durable PostgreSQL. Each binding now keeps up to
`max-in-flight` intake calls running (default 16; `1` keeps the previous behaviour). A message is
still accepted only after it is persisted, and duplicates are still absorbed by the inbox. On stop
the engine waits for the calls in flight and settles each; on a lost connection the broker
redelivers what was not settled and the inbox absorbs the copies.

On the new intake bench (one Artemis queue, durable PostgreSQL, each message starting an instance
that parks; 2,000 messages preloaded), one binding:

| `max-in-flight` | 1 | 4 | 8 | **16 (default)** | 32 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| messages/s | 222.9 | 223.9 | 358.1 | **513.0** | 505.6 | 471.4 |

16 is the smallest window within 90% of the plateau; p99 broker-to-accept latency stayed at or
under 7 ms at every steady rate up to 100 messages/s. The fixture's intake is cheap (about 3 ms
per durable start), so a heavier flow gains more from the window and reaches lower absolute
rates.

## FEEL scopes without deep copies

Every FEEL construct that binds a name (a filter, a quantifier, a `for` loop, a context literal, a
user function call) copied the whole variable scope, payload included, once per item. A filter
over a 500-element list in the payload cost a third of a second. These constructs now look names
up through a layered scope holding only the new bindings. Results are identical: the DMN TCK and
the expression suites pass unchanged.

Measured with the new `feel_scope_benches` (a payload of 500 records × 12 fields plus 20
variables), 0.8.2 against 0.8.3:

| Expression | 0.8.2 | 0.8.3 | Faster |
|---|---|---|---|
| `payload.items[amount > 10]` | 497 ms | 2.3 ms | 217× |
| `some i in payload.items satisfies i.flag` | 376 ms | 1.1 ms | 354× |
| `for i in payload.items return i.amount` | 1.32 s | 0.57 ms | 2,311× |
| `sort(payload.items, function(x, y) x.amount < y.amount)` | 4.10 s | 25.9 ms | 159× |

The existing FEEL benches did not regress, and the DMN TCK results are identical.

## Image scan

The base image's findings without a fix (glibc `iconv` and `glob`, OpenSSL `libssl3`) were
re-verified on this binary: it links only `libgcc_s`, `libm`, `libc` and the loader, imports none
of the affected functions, and loads no OpenSSL library. Two new `libssl3` findings without a
Debian fix, CVE-2026-121482 (a crafted CMS or PKCS#7 SignedData message) and CVE-2026-121481 (an
integer overflow in `EVP_EncodeBlock`), are unreachable for the same reason; the Kafka client's
compiled-in OpenSSL parses no CMS or PKCS#7 and base64-encodes only short SASL and OAUTHBEARER
values. All are time-boxed in `.trivyignore.yaml`, to 2026-12-16.

## Known

- **`SUTRA.INBOUND.CAPABILITY_MISMATCH` answers HTTP 500.** Unchanged from 0.6.23; a later release
  will answer it with 415.
